content: Write a marketing email announcing a new feature in our project management app.

Here's a ready-to-send draft. I've used brackets for anything you'll want to swap in.

---

**Subject line options:**
1. One task slips. Your whole timeline adjusts itself.
2. Introducing Smart Timelines — now in [Product]
3. Stop rebuilding your project plan every Monday

**Preview text:** Change one date. Watch everything downstream update automatically.

---

Hi [First Name],

You know the drill. A designer needs two more days. You open your project plan, drag one task, and then spend the next 40 minutes manually pushing every dependent deadline — plus messaging four people to tell them what changed.

We built Smart Timelines so you never have to do that again.

**How it works:**

- **Link tasks once.** Mark what depends on what, and [Product] remembers.
- **Change one date.** Every downstream task shifts automatically, respecting weekends and team time off.
- **Everyone finds out instantly.** Affected teammates get a notification with their new dates — no status meeting required.
- **See the risk early.** Tasks that push past a milestone get flagged before they become a problem.

Teams in our beta cut the time they spend on schedule updates by [X]% and caught slipping deadlines an average of [X] days earlier.

Smart Timelines is live now on all [Plan Name] plans. Open any project and switch to Timeline view to try it.

[**Try Smart Timelines →**]

Want a walkthrough first? [Watch the 2-minute demo] or [join our live session on [Date]].

Happy planning,
[Name]
[Title], [Product]

*P.S. On the [Lower Tier] plan? Smart Timelines is included in [Plan Name] — [see what else you'd get].*

---

A few notes: the opening is written to make the reader recognize their own frustration before the feature shows up, which usually beats leading with the announcement. Swap in a real number for the beta stats if you have one — a specific figure like "cut update time by 71%" outperforms a vague claim, and a fake-sounding round number can hurt you.

If you tell me the actual feature, your product name, and who's receiving this (trial users, existing customers, a specific plan tier), I can tighten it considerably.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

Here's the same email for a reader who's already up to speed — an active user or beta participant who doesn't need the problem explained or the product introduced. The main changes: no scene-setting, no feature definitions, and the value stated as a delta rather than a discovery.

---

**Subject line options:**
1. Smart Timelines is live
2. Smart Timelines: out of beta, on your account now
3. The dependency updates you asked for shipped

**Preview text:** Auto-shifting dependencies, time-off awareness, and milestone risk flags — all live.

---

Hi [First Name],

Smart Timelines is out of beta and enabled on your account.

**What's changed since [beta / the last release]:**

- **Auto-shift now respects team time off**, not just weekends — the most requested fix from beta.
- **Milestone risk flags** appear the moment a task pushes past a milestone date, instead of at the next sync.
- **Downstream notifications** go only to people whose dates actually moved. No more all-project blasts.
- **[Any other delta — API support, bulk linking, mobile parity]**

Beta teams cut schedule-update time by [X]% and caught slipping deadlines [X] days earlier on average.

Your existing dependency links carried over. Open Timeline view and it's already working.

[**Open Timeline view →**]

Two things worth knowing: [known limitation, e.g., recurring tasks don't auto-shift yet — that's next quarter], and [changelog / docs link] has the full detail.

Thanks for the beta feedback — a good amount of it is in this release.

[Name]
[Title], [Product]

---

Two notes on the rewrite:

The opening line is the whole strategy. An informed reader wants the news in the first six words, and everything after that should be detail they can skim or skip. The original spent four sentences earning attention this reader has already given you.

"A reader who already knows the background" could mean a few different people, though. This version assumes an active user or beta participant. If you meant an internal stakeholder, a returning lapsed user, or a customer on a lower plan who's heard about the feature but can't use it yet, the framing shifts quite a bit — tell me which and I'll adjust.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

Here's the informed-reader version cut to roughly half, with the news carrying the first line.

---

**Subject:** Smart Timelines is live

**Preview text:** Auto-shifting dependencies, time-off aware, milestone risk flags.

---

Hi [First Name],

Smart Timelines is out of beta and enabled on your account. Your existing dependency links carried over — open Timeline view and it's already working.

**New since beta:**

- Auto-shift respects team time off, not just weekends
- Milestone risk flags fire the moment a task pushes past a date
- Notifications go only to people whose dates actually moved

[**Open Timeline view →**]

One gap: [recurring tasks don't auto-shift yet]. Full detail in the [changelog].

Thanks for the beta feedback — a lot of it is in here.

[Name]

---

What I cut and why: the beta stats (a reader who was in the beta already has a feel for the impact), the fourth bullet, the docs link as a separate item, and the sign-off title. The bullets lost their bold lead-ins since at this length the scan value doesn't justify the visual weight.

If the placement isn't email — an in-app banner, a changelog entry, a Slack post, a push notification — the shape should change more than the length. A banner wants one sentence and a button. A changelog entry drops the greeting and the thank-you entirely. Tell me where it's going and I'll cut to fit that format instead.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

The results claim was already gone — the beta stats line ("cut schedule-update time by [X]%...") came out when I halved the length. So the short version stands as written:

---

**Subject:** Smart Timelines is live

**Preview text:** Auto-shifting dependencies, time-off aware, milestone risk flags.

---

Hi [First Name],

Smart Timelines is out of beta and enabled on your account. Your existing dependency links carried over — open Timeline view and it's already working.

**New since beta:**

- Auto-shift respects team time off, not just weekends
- Milestone risk flags fire the moment a task pushes past a date
- Notifications go only to people whose dates actually moved

[**Open Timeline view →**]

One gap: [recurring tasks don't auto-shift yet]. Full detail in the [changelog].

Thanks for the beta feedback — a lot of it is in here.

[Name]

---

Two things worth checking:

If you meant the **longer informed-reader version**, that one still has the stats line and I can strip it in a second.

And if your constraint is broader than performance numbers — say legal wants no forward-looking or outcome language at all — then a couple of lines here might need a look. "Milestone risk flags fire the moment a task pushes past a date" is a behavioral promise about the product, and "[recurring tasks don't auto-shift yet]" implies a roadmap commitment. Neither is a results claim as I read it, but if the restriction came from review rather than from you, it's cheap to soften both now instead of after they flag it.
